claim: Malat1 is a highly evolutionarily conserved and abundant nuclear lncRNA.
source: Malat1 (metastasis associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1) is a highly evolutionarily conserved and abundant nuclear lncRNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the characteristics of Malat1.

claim: Malat1 is a 6.8 kilo-nucleotide RNA Polymerase II transcript from mouse chromosome 19.
source: It is a 6.8 kilo-nucleotide RNA Polymerase II transcript from mouse chromosome 19 (8.9 kilo-nucleotide from human chromosome 11).
evidence: This is a direct statement providing specific information about the size and chromosomal location of Malat1.

claim: Malat1 is an 8.9 kilo-nucleotide transcript from human chromosome 11.
source: It is a 6.8 kilo-nucleotide RNA Polymerase II transcript from mouse chromosome 19 (8.9 kilo-nucleotide from human chromosome 11).
evidence: This is a direct statement providing specific information about the size and chromosomal location of human Malat1.

claim: Malat1 was initially recognized as a gene showing specific upregulation in metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer cells.
source: As one of the first discovered lncRNAs, Malat1 was initially recognized as a gene showing specific upregulation in metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer cells (Gutschner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gutschner et al., 2013.

claim: Malat1 has been associated with the growth and metastasis of different cancers, such as lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and breast cancer.
source: Subsequent studies found a variety of associations between Malat1 and the growth and metastasis of different cancers, such as lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and breast cancer (Yoshimoto et al., 2016; Kwok et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yoshimoto et al., 2016 and Kwok et al., 2018.

claim: Malat1 knockout mice appeared to have no defects in nuclear speckle assembly or pre-mRNA splicing.
source: In physiological settings, although Malat1 was reported to be a key component of nuclear speckle and a regulator of alternative pre-mRNA splicing in in vitro studies, Malat1 knockout (KO) mice surprisingly appeared to have no defects in nuclear speckle assembly or pre-mRNA splicing (Nakagawa et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012; Eißmann et al., 2012; Tripathi et al., 2010; Ip and Nakagawa, 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies on Malat1 knockout mice.

claim: Adult Malat1-/- mice do not show growth retardation or macroscopic differences.
source: Adult mice with Malat1 deficiency (Malat1-/- on C57BL/6 background) do not show growth retardation or macroscopic differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This statement is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing body weight data.

claim: Malat1-/- mice exhibit significantly reduced bone mass compared with wild type littermate controls.
source: Adult mice with Malat1 deficiency (Malat1-/- on C57BL/6 background) do not show growth retardation or macroscopic differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but exhibit significantly reduced bone mass compared with wild type littermate controls (WT; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Malat1-/- mice show markedly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), number (Tb.N.), bone mineral density (BMD) and connectivity density (Conn-Dens.), and increased trabecular spacing (Tb. Sp) in both male and female mice.
source: μCT analysis showed markedly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), number (Tb.N.), bone mineral density (BMD) and connectivity density (Conn-Dens.), and increased trabecular spacing (Tb. Sp) in both male and female Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by μCT analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cortical bone appears normal in Malat1-/- mice.
source: Cortical bone appears normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Osteoclastic bone resorption was significantly enhanced in Malat1-/- mice indicated by the elevated numbers and surfaces of osteoclasts.
source: Osteoclastic bone resorption was significantly enhanced in Malat1-/- mice indicated by the elevated numbers and surfaces of osteoclasts (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by TRAP staining and histomorphometric analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Osteoblastic bone formation was dramatically suppressed by Malat1 deficiency.
source: However, osteoblastic bone formation was not accordingly enhanced but instead was dramatically suppressed by Malat1 deficiency (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1E–H.

claim: Malat1 absence notably inhibited both mineral apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR/BS) in Malat1-/- mice.
source: Bone dynamic histomorphometric analysis by calcein double labeling showed that Malat1 absence notably inhibited both mineral apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR/BS) in Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This statement is supported by calcein double labeling data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Osteoblast surfaces, numbers, and osteoid formed beneath osteoblasts were significantly reduced in Malat1-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, osteoblast parameters, such as osteoblast surfaces and numbers, as well as osteoid formed beneath osteoblasts were significantly reduced in Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This statement is supported by histological staining and morphometric analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The serum osteoblastic bone formation marker P1NP was decreased in Malat1-/- mice.
source: The serum osteoblastic bone formation marker P1NP was decreased, while osteoclastic bone resorption marker TRAP was increased, in Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1I).
evidence: This statement is supported by serum marker data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The serum osteoclastic bone resorption marker TRAP was increased in Malat1-/- mice.
source: The serum osteoblastic bone formation marker P1NP was decreased, while osteoclastic bone resorption marker TRAP was increased, in Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1I).
evidence: This statement is supported by serum marker data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The lack of Malat1 suppresses osteogenesis and bone formation in mice.
source: These results indicate that the lack of Malat1 suppresses osteogenesis and bone formation in mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Malat1 deficiency uncouples osteoclastic bone resorption and osteoblastic bone formation, leading to markedly reduced bone mass.
source: Moreover, Malat1 deficiency uncouples osteoclastic bone resorption and osteoblastic bone formation, leading to markedly reduced bone mass.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing both increased osteoclast activity and decreased osteoblast activity in Malat1-/- mice.

claim: Malat1 is a novel bone remodeling regulator in bone homeostasis.
source: Our data thus identify Malat1 as a novel bone remodeling regulator in bone homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing Malat1's effects on bone remodeling.

claim: Malat1 deficiency in osteoblasts significantly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), number (Tb.N.), thickness (Tb. Th), bone mineral density (BMD) and connectivity density (Conn-Dens.), and increased trabecular spacing (Tb. Sp) in Malat1 cKOOcn mice.
source: Malat1 deficiency in osteoblasts significantly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), number (Tb.N.), thickness (Tb. Th), bone mineral density (BMD) and connectivity density (Conn-Dens.), and increased trabecular spacing (Tb. Sp) in Malat1 cKOOcn mice (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This statement is supported by μCT analysis data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: There are no obvious changes in cortical bone phenotype in Malat1 cKOOcn mice.
source: There are no obvious changes in cortical bone phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mineral apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR/BS) were both lower in Malat1 cKOOcn mice than the controls.
source: Furthermore, mineral apposition rate (MAR) and bone formation rate (BFR/BS) were both lower in Malat1 cKOOcn mice than the controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: This statement is supported by calcein double labeling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Malat1 deficiency in osteoblasts led to decreased osteoblast numbers and surfaces in vivo.
source: In parallel, Malat1 deficiency in osteoblasts led to decreased osteoblast numbers and surfaces in vivo (Figure 2D).
evidence: This statement is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The serum osteoblastic bone formation marker P1NP was decreased in Malat1 cKOOcn mice.
source: The serum osteoblastic bone formation marker P1NP was decreased in Malat1 cKOOcn mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by serum marker data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Malat1 cKOOcn mice exhibit osteoporotic phenotype with reduced bone formation, which is consistent with Malat1-/- mice.
source: These results indicate that Malat1 cKOOcn mice exhibit osteoporotic phenotype with reduced bone formation, which is consistent with Malat1-/- mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing Malat1 cKOOcn and Malat1-/- mice.

claim: Malat1 is a cell-intrinsic osteogenic regulator that promotes osteoblastic bone formation.
source: Therefore, Malat1 is a cell-intrinsic osteogenic regulator that promotes osteoblastic bone formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the osteoblast-specific conditional knockout data.

claim: Malat1 binds to β-catenin in osteoblasts.
source: In this study, we performed both Chromatin isolation by RNA purification (ChIRP) assay (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) assay (Figure 3C) to determine the interaction between Malat1 and β-catenin. The results obtained by these two approaches clearly show that Malat1 binds to β-catenin in osteoblasts (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This statement is supported by ChIRP and RIP assay data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Malat1 deficiency did not significantly affect nuclear localization of β-catenin stimulated by Wnt3a.
source: Next, we asked whether Malat1 regulates β-catenin nuclear translocation in response to Wnt3a. We did not find that Malat1 deficiency significantly affects nuclear localization of β-catenin stimulated by Wnt3a (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Malat1 deficiency significantly reduced the transcriptional activity of β-catenin in response to Wnt3a stimulation.
source: We then performed Luciferase assay to examine whether Malat1 modulates the transcriptional activity of β-catenin. The results showed that Malat1 deficiency significantly reduced the transcriptional activity of β-catenin in response to Wnt3a stimulation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This statement is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The expression levels of β-catenin target genes, such as Axin2, Ccnd1, Lef1 and Myc, were substantially lower in Malat1-/- cells than WT controls.
source: In line with this, the expression levels of β-catenin target genes, such as Axin2, Ccnd1, Lef1 and Myc, were substantially lower in Malat1-/- cells than WT controls (Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Malat1 is a key regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway that is important for osteoblasts.
source: Our findings indicate that Malat1 is a key regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway that is important for osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing Malat1's effects on β-catenin activity and target gene expression.

claim: Malat1 acts as a scaffold to tether β-catenin in nuclei to implement its positive regulation of β-catenin activity.
source: Since Malat1 is a nuclear lncRNA, these data also suggest that Malat1 acts as a scaffold to tether β-catenin in nuclei to implement its positive regulation of β-catenin activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on Malat1's nuclear localization and its binding to β-catenin.

claim: There is no significant difference in osteoclast differentiation and mineral resorption between WT and Malat1-/- BMM cultures.
source: Surprisingly, there is no significant difference in osteoclast differentiation and mineral resorption between WT and Malat1-/- BMM cultures (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This statement is supported by in vitro osteoclast differentiation data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The expression of osteoclastogenic transcription factors and osteoclast marker genes was similar between WT and Malat1-/- cultures.
source: Moreover, the expression of osteoclastogenic transcription factors and osteoclast marker genes was similar between WT and Malat1-/- cultures (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: There is no significant difference in bone mass between Malat1 cKOLyz2 mice and their littermate control Lyz2Cre(+) mice.
source: However, there is no significant difference in bone mass between Malat1 cKOLyz2 mice and their littermate control Lyz2Cre(+) mice (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by μCT analysis data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Malat1 expressed in osteoclastic lineage cells does not affect osteoclastogenesis.
source: These results demonstrate that Malat1 expressed in osteoclastic lineage cells does not affect osteoclastogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro and in vivo data showing no effect of Malat1 deletion in osteoclast lineage cells.

claim: Malat1 inhibits osteoclastogenesis in a non-autonomous manner in vivo.
source: Therefore, Malat1 inhibits osteoclastogenesis in a non-autonomous manner in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing that Malat1 affects osteoclasts through other cell types, not directly.

claim: Malat1 deletion in osteoblasts significantly enhanced osteoclast numbers and surfaces in vivo.
source: We first looked at osteoclast phenotype in Malat1 cKOOcn mice, and found that Malat1 deletion in osteoblasts significantly enhanced osteoclast numbers and surfaces in vivo (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by TRAP staining and histomorphometric analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The serum osteoclastic bone resorption marker TRAP was increased in Malat1 cKOOcn mice.
source: The serum osteoclastic bone resorption marker TRAP was increased in Malat1 cKOOcn mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by serum marker data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Malat1 affects osteoclast formation through crosstalk between osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
source: This finding indicates that Malat1 affects osteoclast formation through crosstalk between osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that osteoblast-specific Malat1 deletion affects osteoclasts.

claim: More osteoclasts formed in the co-cultures with Malat1-/- osteoblasts than WT osteoblasts.
source: Interestingly, we found that more osteoclasts formed in the co-cultures with Malat1-/- osteoblasts than WT osteoblasts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: OPG expression was markedly lower in the Malat1-/- osteoblasts than the WT control cells.
source: We found that OPG expression was markedly lower in the Malat1-/- osteoblasts than the WT control cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: OPG but not RANKL was down-regulated in Malat1-/- osteoblasts, leading to a higher RANKL/OPG ratio in Malat1-/- osteoblasts than WT controls.
source: Our results showed that OPG but not RANKL was down-regulated in Malat1-/- osteoblasts, leading to a higher RANKL/OPG ratio in Malat1-/- osteoblasts than WT controls (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The OPG level in serum in Malat1-/- mice is similar to that in WT controls.
source: Indeed, the OPG level in serum in Malat1-/- mice is similar to that in WT controls (Figure 5G).
evidence: This statement is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: OPG level in bone marrow was drastically decreased in Malat1-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: However, OPG level in bone marrow was drastically decreased in Malat1-/- mice compared to WT mice (Figure 5H).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Malat1 deletion in Malat1-/- bone marrow enabled more osteoclastogenesis than WT bone marrow in whole bone marrow cultures with M-CSF and RANKL.
source: In the whole bone marrow cultures with M-CSF and RANKL (Figure 5I), Malat1 deletion in Malat1-/- bone marrow enabled more osteoclastogenesis than WT bone marrow, which is consistent with the in vivo findings.
evidence: This statement is supported by bone marrow culture data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Recombinant OPG can lead to osteoclast formation in Malat1-/- osteoblasts and WT bone marrow cocultures comparable to that in WT osteoblasts and WT bone marrow cocultures without extra OPG.
source: Extra OPG can lead to osteoclast formation in Malat1-/- osteoblasts and WT bone marrow cocultures comparable to that in WT osteoblasts and WT bone marrow cocultures without extra OPG (Figure 5J column 1 vs 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The decreased OPG level in Malat1-deficient osteoblasts plays a significant role in the excessive osteoclast formation in Malat1-/- mice and Malat1 cKOOcn mice.
source: These results collectively support that the decreased OPG level in Malat1-deficient osteoblasts plays a significant role in the excessive osteoclast formation in Malat1-/- mice (Figure 1C and D) and Malat1 cKOOcn mice (Figure 5A), as illustrated in Figure 7.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OPG rescue experiments and the observed osteoclast phenotypes.

claim: Chondrocytes express a high level of OPG in the analyzed cells from bone.
source: We analyzed a bone scRNAseq dataset (GSE128423) (Baryawno et al., 2019). Except for osteoblasts as expected, we surprisingly found that chondrocytes express a high level of OPG in the analyzed cells from bone (Figure 6A-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: OPG expression level in Malat1-/- chondrocytes was approximately 50% less compared to that in WT cells.
source: Moreover, OPG expression level in Malat1-/- chondrocytes was approximately 50% less compared to that in WT cells (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: RANKL (encoded by Tnfsf11) is nearly undetectable in chondrocytes.
source: RANKL (encoded by Tnfsf11) is nearly undetectable in chondrocytes (Figure 6F).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The chondrocyte marker genes, including Sox9, Acan and Col2a1, were not affected by Malat1.
source: The chondrocyte marker genes, including Sox9, Acan and Col2a1, were not affected by Malat1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Chondrocytes are an important cellular source of OPG highly expressed in bone, which is critically regulated by Malat1.
source: These data show that chondrocytes are an important cellular source of OPG highly expressed in bone, which is critically regulated by Malat1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNAseq analysis and the expression data in chondrocytes.

claim: The expression of β-catenin target genes, such as Tcf7, Lef1, and Jag1, was approximately 50% lower in Malat1-/- chondrocytes than that in WT cells.
source: In addition to OPG, we observed that the expression of other β-catenin target genes, such as Tcf7, Lef1, and Jag1, was approximately 50% lower in Malat1-/- chondrocytes than that in WT cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This statement is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Malat1 positively regulates β-catenin activity in chondrocytes.
source: This suggests that, similar to osteoblasts, Malat1 positively regulates β-catenin activity in chondrocytes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing decreased β-catenin target gene expression in Malat1-/- chondrocytes.

claim: Malat1 deficiency drastically decreased Jagged1 protein expression in chondrocytes.
source: Following this observation, we evaluated the protein expression levels of Jagged1, and found that Malat1 deficiency drastically decreased Jagged1 protein expression in chondrocytes (Figure 6I).
evidence: This statement is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The decreased OPG and Jagged1 production in Malat1-/- chondrocytes contributes to the enhanced osteoclast formation and low bone mass in Malat1-/- mice.
source: These results collectively indicate that the decreased OPG and Jagged1 production in Malat1-/- chondrocytes also contributes to the enhanced osteoclast formation and low bone mass in Malat1-/- mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression data in chondrocytes and the known functions of OPG and Jagged1.

claim: Malat1 links the activities of chondrocytes and osteoclasts through β-catenin-OPG/Jagged1 axis.
source: Thus, Malat1 links the activities of chondrocytes and osteoclasts through β-catenin-OPG/Jagged1 axis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing Malat1's regulation of OPG and Jagged1 in chondrocytes and their effects on osteoclasts.

claim: Malat1 deficiency in both Malat1-/- mice and Malat1 cKOOcn mice significantly disturbed the bone regeneration at 21 days post-fracture, indicated by significantly decreased bone mass in the newly formed callus.
source: In a femoral midshaft fracture model (Xu et al., 2018), we found that Malat1 deficiency in both Malat1-/- mice and Malat1 cKOOcn mice significantly disturbed the bone regeneration at 21 days post-fracture, indicated by significantly decreased bone mass in the newly formed callus (Figure 8).
evidence: This statement is supported by fracture healing data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Malat1 in osteoblasts plays an important role in enhancing bone regeneration in fracture healing.
source: These results indicate that Malat1 in osteoblasts plays an important role in enhancing bone regeneration in fracture healing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fracture healing data in Malat1-/- and Malat1 cKOOcn mice.

claim: Over 75% of the human genome is transcribed.
source: Recent genome-wide transcriptome analyses revealed that over 75% of the human genome is transcribed, among which about 95% are transcripts without coding capacity.
evidence: This is a statement about genome-wide transcriptome analyses.

claim: About 95% of transcribed human genome are transcripts without coding capacity.
source: Recent genome-wide transcriptome analyses revealed that over 75% of the human genome is transcribed, among which about 95% are transcripts without coding capacity.
evidence: This is a statement about genome-wide transcriptome analyses.

claim: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a relatively new category of non-coding RNAs (≥500 nucleotides).
source: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) emerge as a relatively new category of non-coding RNAs (≥500 nucleotides Mattick et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a definition of lncRNAs with a citation to Mattick et al., 2023.

claim: lncRNAs can perform diverse regulatory roles in regulation of gene expression.
source: It is now widely accepted that lncRNAs can perform diverse regulatory roles in regulation of gene expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the accepted functions of lncRNAs.

claim: lncRNAs are enriched in the nucleus and/or cytoplasm and possess the ability to interact with versatile biomolecules, including various proteins, chromosomal DNAs and RNAs.
source: lncRNAs are enriched in the nucleus and/or cytoplasm and possess the ability to interact with versatile biomolecules, including various proteins, chromosomal DNAs and RNAs.
evidence: This is a statement about the localization and interaction capabilities of lncRNAs.

claim: lncRNAs regulate gene expression and function by diverse mechanisms, such as functioning as scaffolds for transcriptional and chromatin-modifying complex assemblies, as enhancers or decoys regulating gene transcription, and as cis-acting or trans-acting regulators involved in gene expression and epigenetic regulation.
source: Therefore, in contrast to miRNAs, lncRNAs regulate gene expression and function by diverse mechanisms, such as functioning as scaffolds for transcriptional and chromatin-modifying complex assemblies, as enhancers or decoys regulating gene transcription, and as cis-acting or trans-acting regulators involved in gene expression and epigenetic regulation (Batista and Chang, 2013; Quinn and Chang, 2016; Smith and Mattick, 2017; Rinn and Chang, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing lncRNA mechanisms.

claim: lncRNAs are druggable targets.
source: Importantly, lncRNAs are druggable targets, and identification of the functional importance of lncRNAs has unveiled new diagnostic and therapeutic opportunities for human diseases, such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and genetic disorders (Batista and Chang, 2013; Cech and Steitz, 2014; Schmitt and Chang, 2017; Modarresi et al., 2012; Shappell, 2008; Tham et al., 2015; Wheeler et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations about lncRNAs as therapeutic targets.

claim: β-catenin is a central transcriptional factor in canonical Wnt signaling pathway, and plays an important role in positively regulating osteoblast differentiation and function.
source: β-catenin is a central transcriptional factor in canonical Wnt signaling pathway, and plays an important role in positively regulating osteoblast differentiation and function (Zhong et al., 2014; Chen and Long, 2013; Holmen et al., 2005; Kramer et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014; Monroe et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations about β-catenin's role in osteoblasts.

claim: Previous reports observed a link between Malat1 and β-catenin signaling pathway in cancers.
source: Previous reports observed a link between Malat1 and β-catenin signaling pathway in cancers Li et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Osteoprotegerin (OPG), encoded by Tnfrsf11b, is a β-catenin target.
source: Osteoprotegerin (OPG), encoded by Tnfrsf11b, is a β-catenin target (Boyce et al., 2005; Glass et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Boyce et al., 2005 and Glass et al., 2005.

claim: OPG is a secreted factor that acts as a RANKL decoy receptor to block RANKL activity, thereby suppressing osteoclast formation and bone resorption.
source: OPG is a secreted factor that acts as a RANKL decoy receptor to block RANKL activity, thereby suppressing osteoclast formation and bone resorption (Simonet et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Simonet et al., 1997.

claim: RANKL-OPG axis is a typical bone remodeling mediator through impacting osteoclastogenesis, and RANKL/OPG ratio is usually an indicator for osteoclastogenic/bone resorption potential and status.
source: RANKL-OPG axis is a typical bone remodeling mediator through impacting osteoclastogenesis, and RANKL/OPG ratio is usually an indicator for osteoclastogenic/bone resorption potential and status (Boyce and Xing, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Boyce and Xing, 2008.

claim: Locally produced OPG in bone, but not the serum OPG, is a critical inhibitor of osteoclast formation and bone resorption.
source: Recent literature demonstrates that locally produced OPG in bone, but not the serum OPG, is a critical inhibitor of osteoclast formation and bone resorption (Tsukasaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsukasaki et al., 2020.

claim: Jagged1 is not only a Notch ligand but also an inhibitor of osteoclastogenesis.
source: The decreased expression of Jagged1 in Malat1-/- chondrocytes drew our attention, as Jagged1 is not only a Notch ligand (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009) but also an inhibitor of osteoclastogenesis (Bai et al., 2008; Zhao, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kopan and Ilagan, 2009; Bai et al., 2008; and Zhao, 2017.

claim: Bone homeostasis in adulthood is mainly maintained by an active bone remodeling process, which requires a delicate balance between osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and osteoblast-mediated bone formation.
source: Bone homeostasis in adulthood is mainly maintained by an active bone remodeling process, which requires a delicate balance between osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and osteoblast-mediated bone formation.
evidence: This is a statement about bone homeostasis and remodeling.

claim: Bone tissues undergo constant remodeling, during which bone resorption and formation are usually coupled to ensure that osteoclast-generated resorption lacunae are filled with new bone produced by osteoblasts.
source: Bone tissues undergo constant remodeling, during which bone resorption and formation are usually coupled to ensure that osteoclast-generated resorption lacunae are filled with new bone produced by osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a statement about bone remodeling coupling.

claim: There exists a variety of crosstalk between two major bone cell types, bone-resorbing osteoclasts and bone-forming osteoblasts, as well as other cells.
source: There exists a variety of crosstalk between two major bone cell types, bone-resorbing osteoclasts and bone-forming osteoblasts, as well as other cells. The intricate cellular crosstalk coordinately couples the activities of different cells to maintain bone homeostasis during remodeling (Sims and Martin, 2014; Raggatt and Partridge, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sims and Martin, 2014 and Raggatt and Partridge, 2010.

claim: Malat1 acts as an intrinsic regulator in osteoblasts to promote osteogenesis.
source: Mechanistically, Malat1 acts as an intrinsic regulator in osteoblasts to promote osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract describing the study's findings.

claim: Malat1 does not directly affect osteoclastogenesis but inhibits osteoclastogenesis in a non-autonomous manner in vivo via integrating crosstalk between multiple cell types, including osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and chondrocytes.
source: Interestingly, Malat1 does not directly affect osteoclastogenesis but inhibits osteoclastogenesis in a non-autonomous manner in vivo via integrating crosstalk between multiple cell types, including osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and chondrocytes.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract describing the study's findings.

claim: Malat1 serves as a central regulator by binding to β-catenin and functioning through the β-catenin-OPG/Jagged1 pathway in osteoblasts and chondrocytes.
source: Our findings substantiate the existence of a novel remodeling network in which Malat1 serves as a central regulator by binding to β-catenin and functioning through the β-catenin-OPG/Jagged1 pathway in osteoblasts and chondrocytes.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract describing the study's findings.

claim: Both Malat1 KO and conditional KO mice in the osteoblast lineage exhibit significant osteoporosis.
source: We found that both Malat1 KO and conditional KO mice in the osteoblast lineage exhibit significant osteoporosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract describing the study's findings.

claim: In pathological conditions, Malat1 significantly promotes bone regeneration in fracture healing.
source: In pathological conditions, Malat1 significantly promotes bone regeneration in fracture healing.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract describing the study's findings.
